The school bus was stuck in traffic outside the zoo, and the fan above the back seats had stopped. Everyone was hot and cranky. The driver kept honking. Then someone at the back started a chant: "Squeaky, squeaky!" It was for Gurpreet, whose voice had begun to crack.
Jomon would never say that to Gurpreet's face. They sat together in maths. But twenty voices were chanting, and in the crowd of heads nobody could tell who was who. Jomon chanted too, laughing.
Gurpreet stared out of the window with red ears.
Ma'am turned round from the front seat. "Enough. Every one of you." She walked down the aisle and sat beside Gurpreet. Jomon stopped, his face burning.

qa.a: It was stuck in traffic outside the zoo.

qa.q: What could Jomon do the next day?
qa.a: He could say sorry to Gurpreet on his own, without the crowd, and refuse to join the chant if it starts again.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurpreet when twenty voices chant at him?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels embarrassed and alone, staring out of the window with red ears while even a friend joins in.

Sabina was not a mean girl. Everyone said so. So nobody expected her to be part of it.
It began in the corridor after the bell. Five girls from her class started flicking paper balls at Ishita's new short haircut, laughing, "Boy cut! Boy cut!"
Sabina had her own paper ball in her hand before she knew why. It was easy. Nobody was looking at her. They were all one giggling crowd. She flicked it.
Ishita turned. Her eyes went straight to Sabina, the only one she had ever shared a tiffin with.
The ball dropped from Sabina's other hand. Suddenly she was not part of a crowd. She was just Sabina, and Ishita had seen her.

qa.a: They flicked paper balls at Ishita's new short haircut.

qa.q: What did Sabina feel when Ishita's eyes went straight to her?
qa.a: She felt exposed and ashamed, as if the crowd had vanished and she was suddenly seen as herself.

qa.q: What small step could Sabina take now?
qa.a: She could go to Ishita, say sorry and tell the other girls to stop, instead of hiding back in the group.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when she sees Sabina among the girls?
qa.a: Ishita is likely hurt and betrayed, because a friend she shared a tiffin with was part of the teasing.

grounding: Shows a kind child joining group teasing because in a giggling crowd nobody seems to be looking at her, until the target looks straight at her.

Shalini, you asked why I've been weird all week. Okay. I'm Chetan, and I did something I'm not proud of.
There's this anonymous page for our school. Someone posted a video of a girl from Class 11 dancing at the annual day. The comments were horrible, and I scrolled and laughed. Then I typed one too. Something about her looking like a wobbling doll.

Vijay's phone battery was at nine per cent, and his chemistry exam was the next morning. He missed the penalty at 5 pm. By 7, someone had put the clip online.
By 8 there were eighty comments. By 9, strangers were messaging him directly. "Loser." "Quit football." Names he didn't know. He tried replying to one, then another. More came. There was no single person to talk to.
He sat on the hostel stairs, shaking. His roommate Jeevan found him there and saw the screen.
"Come," Jeevan said. They went straight to the warden's room. The warden sat with Vijay, saved screenshots, turned off his notifications, reported the account, and said, "This is not your fault. We'll speak to the coach in the morning."

Tenzin read her poem aloud in the Delhi school's assembly on Friday. By lunch, someone had made a meme of her face mid-word and posted it on the class group.
Then it spread to other sections. Stickers. Voice notes mimicking her. Forty, sixty, a hundred messages. She didn't even know most of the numbers.

Uday felt the pull; the noise made everything seem funny. Then he looked at Saurabh, who was holding a second chair above his head and grinning.
"Saurabh. The guard's inside that cabin."

You asked why I left the hostel Holi early. Here's what happened.

Dear Dilnaz,
You asked me about the march. I want to tell you about the moment I stepped aside.
We were marching for the new bus route, peacefully, hundreds of us. Near the market, someone started a chant against a shopkeeper who had spoken against the route. Then people began banging on his shutter and shouting names at his son.
I had my placard. I believed in the cause. But I thought: my name comes with me here. If I shout that, it's me shouting it.
So I stepped out of the line and stood beside the shop. Two others joined me. After a minute the crowd moved on.
The bus route still matters to me. So does that boy's face.
Lalremsiami

qa.a: It showed a different choice, two others joined, and the crowd moved on without hurting the family more.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper's son have felt when people shouted his name?
qa.a: He likely felt frightened and humiliated by a crowd blaming him for his father's view.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a march reminding themselves that their name travels with them, and stepping aside when the crowd turns on a family.

Chandrika, you know the anonymous feedback forum at work? Let me tell you why I stopped using it the way others do. I'm Lalit, by the way, in case the podcast listeners forget.
Last month, a colleague made a small mistake in a report. Within an hour, the forum had thirty posts mocking her. "Clueless." "Hire better." Nobody signed anything.
I was about to add one. Then I thought: if I wouldn't say it with my name on it, why say it at all?
So I wrote, under my own name, "It was a small error. She fixed it in an hour. Let's move on." And I stopped reading the thread.
Two people messaged me privately to say thanks.

passage:
Parul, you asked why I've gone so quiet at work. I'm Tanvir, and here's how it happened.
In my first month I used to speak in meetings. Then one day I disagreed with my manager about a timeline. She didn't shout. She just stopped copying me on emails for a week.
Now I watch everything. If she comes in with her coffee, it's a good day. If she comes in without it, I keep my head down. I've learned to say "Yes, good idea" before she finishes a sentence.
Last week I had a better plan for the client, and I didn't mention it.
I feel smaller every month. I don't even recognise my own voice in meetings.

qa.q: What did the manager stop doing for a week?
qa.a: She stopped copying Tanvir on emails for a week.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about not mentioning the better plan?
qa.a: Tanvir feels smaller and a little ashamed, having learned to hide views to stay safe.

qa.q: What small step could Tanvir try to get some voice back?
qa.a: Tanvir could share one idea in writing to the manager, or talk to a trusted senior about how to raise views safely.

qa.q: What would change if the manager welcomed disagreement?
qa.a: Tanvir would feel free to share the better plan, and the client and team might gain from it.

grounding: Shows a junior employee who has learned to read a powerful manager's moods and hide their views, feeling smaller as a result.

passage:
February: Damini joined the design team full of ideas. At her first review, she said Omkar's layout was too cramped. He said nothing. The next week her project was taken away.
April: Damini had learned his signals. A tap of the pen meant stop talking. A long sigh meant change the slide. She watched his face more than her work. When he asked, "Any thoughts?" she said, "It's perfect as it is."
June: A friend from college asked what she was designing. Damini opened her mouth and realised she didn't know what she thought any more. "Whatever Omkar wants," she said, and laughed. It didn't feel funny.

qa.q: What did a tap of Omkar's pen mean?
qa.a: A tap of the pen meant stop talking.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she said "Whatever Omkar wants" and laughed?
qa.a: She felt hollow and uneasy, realising she had lost touch with her own views.

qa.q: What could help Damini now?
qa.a: She could talk to someone she trusts, such as a mentor or HR, and start keeping her own design notes so her views aren't lost.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Damini's silence in reviews?
qa.a: Omkar may see it as agreement and not notice that she has stopped offering ideas.

grounding: Shows a junior employee learning to read a manager's signals, hiding her views to stay safe and feeling smaller over months.

passage:
Disha, you're scared of your new boss? Let your Abbu tell you about Sharma sahib. I'm Yusuf, and at twenty-four I was a junior accountant under him.
He could make the whole room silent by clearing his throat. I learned his moods like weather: a closed door meant storm, tea on his desk meant sunshine. I agreed with everything. I once changed a correct figure because he frowned at it.
One evening I went home and couldn't remember the last time I'd said what I thought. I felt like a shadow.
The next month I found an error in his report. My hands shook. I wrote it in a note, politely, and left it on his desk. He grunted. But he fixed it.

qa.q: What did a closed door mean in Yusuf's weather?
qa.a: A closed door meant storm.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel on the evening he couldn't remember saying what he thought?
qa.a: He felt small and empty, like a shadow of himself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Yusuf's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Leaving a polite note about the error; it let him use his voice in a safe way, and the boss fixed it.

qa.q: How might Sharma sahib have seen the note on his desk?
qa.a: He may have been surprised, but he grunted and fixed the error, which shows he could accept a respectful correction.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a junior employee learning to read a powerful boss's moods and hide his views, and then finding a small safe voice.

passage:
You asked about Leela? Okay. I'm Zeenat. Leela and I joined the marketing team on the same day, ate lunch together every day, and complained together about our old boss.
Then she became team lead. At first nothing changed. By month three, she was interrupting people in meetings. She booked the good conference room for herself without asking. She stopped joining lunch.
Others started gossiping. I didn't want that. So one evening I asked her for tea and said, "You've been cutting people off. I don't think you mean to."
She went quiet. Then she said, "I'm scared I'll fail. The pressure is huge."
I said, "I get it. But we're on your side."

qa.q: What did Leela book for herself without asking?
qa.a: She booked the good conference room for herself without asking.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been feeling before speaking to Leela?
qa.a: Zeenat seemed uneasy and a little nervous, wanting to be honest without hurting a friend.

qa.q: Why might Zeenat's way of raising it help?
qa.a: Zeenat talked privately and kindly instead of gossiping, and also listened to Leela's pressure, so Leela could hear it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How does Leela see her own behaviour once Zeenat names it?
qa.a: Leela admits she feels scared of failing, suggesting the pressure has been pushing her to act this way.

grounding: Shows a peer watching a friend become a manager and stop listening, then gently naming the change instead of gossiping and acknowledging the pressure on her.

passage:
I sat across from Joseph for two years before he was promoted. We were a team: ideas scribbled on the same notepad, shared biryani on Fridays.
After the promotion, he got a cabin. Slowly he changed. In meetings he finished other people's sentences. He started expecting reports on his desk before he asked. Once he snapped at a new joiner, "I don't have time for basic questions."
The others muttered about him at the tea machine. I didn't join in.
Instead, I waited till the end of a Friday and knocked. "Joseph, you've stopped letting people finish. The new joiner was upset."
He rubbed his eyes. "I know. The targets are killing me." He came out and apologised to the new joiner that evening.
I'm Devika. I still sit across from his cabin.

qa.q: What did Joseph snap at the new joiner?
qa.a: He snapped, "I don't have time for basic questions."

qa.q: What might Devika have felt while the others muttered at the tea machine?
qa.a: Devika likely felt uncomfortable and torn, not wanting to gossip about a friend but still worried about the change.

qa.q: What approach did Devika take, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Devika spoke to Joseph privately and named one clear behaviour, so he could hear it and fix it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel after he rubs his eyes and admits the targets are killing him?
qa.a: He likely feels tired and a bit ashamed, but relieved that someone spoke to him directly.

grounding: Shows a peer watching a friend change after promotion, and naming it gently in private while acknowledging the pressure he is under.

passage:
Monday, week one: Dhruv got the team lead post. Akash bought him a cake. Dhruv hugged everyone.
Wednesday, week five: In the stand-up, Dhruv cut Akash off twice. He asked for the window desk, "since leads need focus." Akash noticed people rolling their eyes after the meeting.
Friday, week eight: The juniors were gossiping in the pantry. Akash left and waited for Dhruv at the parking lot instead. "You've been interrupting a lot. You also took the window desk. That's not the Dhruv I know."
Dhruv leaned on his bike. "My manager calls me every evening asking for numbers. I think I'm passing it on."
"Then let's fix it together."

qa.q: What did Akash buy Dhruv?
qa.a: Akash bought him a cake.

qa.q: Why did Akash leave the pantry and wait at the parking lot?
qa.a: Akash felt uncomfortable with the gossip and concerned for Dhruv, wanting to raise it directly and kindly.

qa.q: What would you advise Dhruv after this talk?
qa.a: Dhruv could let people finish in stand-ups, give back the window desk and tell his manager how the pressure is affecting the team.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv to hear this from Akash?
qa.a: Dhruv may feel stung but relieved, since a friend named it privately and he could admit the pressure he's under.

grounding: Shows a peer watching a friend change as a new lead over weeks, and naming it gently instead of gossiping while recognising the pressure on him.

passage:
When I was made project lead last year, at twenty-five, my first fear was turning into the boss I'd hated. I'm Divyansh, and I did three things on purpose.
First, I kept Lalit close. He's my oldest friend at the firm and loves to argue. When I proposed weekend work, he said, "Ask the juniors what it costs them first." I did. Two of them had exams. We moved it.
Second, every Friday I asked the team one question: "What's one thing I did this week that didn't help?"
Third, when the client praised the report, I read out the names of the two juniors who'd built it.
It's not perfect. But I still hear things I don't want to hear, and that feels right.

qa.q: What question did Divyansh ask the team every Friday?
qa.a: "What's one thing I did this week that didn't help?"

qa.q: What was Divyansh afraid of when made project lead?
qa.a: Divyansh was afraid of becoming the kind of boss once hated, and so felt the need to guard against it.

qa.q: Which of Divyansh's habits seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Lalit close is useful, because an honest friend who disagrees catches mistakes like the weekend work before they hurt people.

qa.q: How might the two juniors feel when their names are read out to the client?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and valued, knowing the lead shared the credit.

grounding: Shows a young leader inviting honest feedback, keeping a friend who disagrees, asking what decisions cost juniors and sharing credit.

passage:
Mentor's note, three months into Gautam's first role as shift supervisor.
Gautam is twenty-four and runs a team of nine at the call centre. I've watched him closely. He does something unusual: at the end of each shift, he asks one agent, "What made today harder?" Leela told him that the new break schedule meant she missed her bus. He changed it the next day.
He also keeps a friend from his training batch, who is now a peer, as his "disagree person." They have lunch every week.
When the team hit its target, he sent the regional manager a list of names, not his own.
I've advised him to keep these habits when the pressure rises.

qa.q: How many people are in Gautam's team?
qa.a: He runs a team of nine.

qa.q: What does Gautam's question "What made today harder?" suggest about how he feels toward his team?
qa.a: It suggests he feels curious and caring about his team, wanting to see the costs of his decisions.

qa.q: What habit should Gautam keep as the pressure rises?
qa.a: He should keep asking agents what made the day harder, since it shows the costs of his decisions early.

qa.q: How might Leela feel when the break schedule changes the next day?
qa.a: Leela would likely feel heard and grateful that her problem was fixed so quickly.

grounding: Shows a young leader asking what his decisions cost people below him, keeping a friend who disagrees and sharing credit.

passage:
Wednesday
Today my first month as warehouse lead ended. I'm Manoj, and I want to write this down before I forget why I started.
Pankaj, who has been here longer than me, told me in the canteen that my new loading order makes the old workers walk twice as far. My first reaction was irritation. I'm the lead now. Then I remembered Pankaj was the one who taught me the ropes.
So I walked the route myself this afternoon. He was right. Tomorrow I'll change it and tell everyone Pankaj spotted it.
Note to self: every week, ask one person what my decisions cost them. Keep Pankaj close, even when he annoys me.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say about the new loading order?
qa.a: He said it makes the old workers walk twice as far.

qa.q: What was Manoj's first reaction to Pankaj, and what does it show?
qa.a: Manoj first felt irritated, which shows the pull of feeling important as the new lead.

qa.q: Which choice helps Manoj stay a good lead, and why?
qa.a: Walking the route to check Pankaj's point and then crediting Pankaj keeps Manoj curious about others and shares credit.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when Manoj tells everyone Pankaj spotted it?
qa.a: Pankaj would likely feel respected and valued for speaking up.

grounding: Shows a young leader checking a decision's cost to workers, keeping an honest colleague close and sharing the credit.
